study.title: Exodus 27 - the altar, the court, and the lamp lit before the Lord
study.overview: Exodus 27 completes the instructions of the sanctuary with three foci: the bronze altar for the sacrifices, the court that separates the holy space from the rest of the camp, and the oil for the lamp that should remain lit before the Lord. The chapter shows that the worship of Israel was not improvised: there was order, distinction, priestly mediation and continuity. The altar points to the need for atonement; the court, for the holy separation of the people of God; and the lamp, to the constant light that should remain in the divine presence.

outline.title: The bronze altar for the burnt offerings
outline.explanation: Verses 1 to 8 describe the square altar of acacia wood covered with bronze, with tips in the four corners, own utensils, inner grille and carrying rods. The hollow and portable form shows that the altar would accompany Israel in the desert, and the whole highlights that the sacrifice was central to access to the Lord.

outline.title: The lobby of the tabernacle and its limits
outline.explanation: Verses 9 to 19 regulate the outer courtyard, with twisted linen curtains, columns, bases, capitals, poles, and the curtain of the door. Space is defined with precise measures and distinct materials, marking a visible separation between the sacred and the common, and showing that the cult had ordained and undiscriminate access.

outline.title: Pure olive oil and continuously lit lamp
outline.explanation: Verses 20 and 21 command Israel to bring pure olive oil to keep the lightlight on continually. Aaron and their sons shall arrange the lamps before the Lord, outside the veil, from the evening until the morning, as a perpetual statute. Daily service supports the image of a presence of God that does not erase.

study.context: The chapter resumes the pattern given on the mount and applies it to the tabernacle and its atrium. The notes indicate that the sanctuary is the center, and the text moves out: first the altar, then the courtyard, finally the maintenance of the light. The term translated by "wifinacle of the testimony" can mean the tent of encounter, that is, the sacred space where God is present among his people. The worship is entrusted to the priests, while the people provide the oil and the offerings.
study.theology: Exodus 27 presents a mediated access theology. The altar teaches that the approach of God involves sacrifice and purification; the horns of the altar remind power, refuge and consecration of the sacrificial act. The atrium shows that the holiness of God requires borders: not all enter the same place, and not all is mixed. The lighted lamp without ceasing symbolizes continuity of the presence and vigilance of the cult. The priestly responsibility and the provision of the people reveal that biblical worship is both the gift of God and the duty of the community. In Protestant evangelical reading, the chapter also points to the need for mediation and the permanence of God's light among his people, without confusing the symbol with its later fulfillment.

scholarViews.insight: The tips of the altar seem to have a practical and theological function: they could help to hold the offer, but they are also linked to the idea of mercy, consecration and acceptance in worship.
The atrium is seen as a figure of the church: a separate space from the world, supported by stable columns and marked by purity and distinction.
The commandment on the lamp implies that it must remain lit continually, and that the order of worship is under the responsibility of Aaron and his children.

questions: What does the bronze altar teach about the seriousness of sin and the need for atonement before God?
How do the borders of the atrium help to understand God's holiness without denying its closeness to the people?
How does the continually lit light confront our tendency to treat worship as something occasional and not constant?
study.practice: Separate regular time for a conscious and reverent cult, remembering that the approach of God is not casual. Take both confession and gratitude seriously, and try to maintain a continuous spiritual life, like the lamp that should not go out. It is also worth noting that the community has its part: some bring the oil, others organize the lamp, and all serve the holy order of God.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not unanimously clarify all the technical details of the altar and the grid, nor do they accurately define whether the atrium should be read mainly as a symbol of the church or just as a cultual instruction. There is also no basis in the notes to go beyond a general reading of the tabernacle of the testimony as the tent of meeting. The confessional interpretations presented here are readings, not mandatory conclusions of the text.
